item.title: AkôFlow Hub is alive — publish, discover and reuse workflows
item.description: A step-by-step tour of AkôFlow Hub: explore public experiments, export workflows, publish execution results and import a version into Desktop.
item.content:encoded:
AkôFlow Hub is alive. Open hub.akoflow.com to discover workflows, inspect their graphs and recorded experiments, and bring a published definition into your own AkôFlow Desktop.

You can now share the workflow behind a result, keep its versions together and let someone else start from the same definition. Here is the complete journey: discover → export → publish → import → prepare a local run.

Open full resolution ↗

What is available today?​

The public Hub brings together workflow definitions, README instructions, immutable workflow versions, executable-image references and recorded execution results. Depending on what the author included, an experiment can also show activity observations, timing, resource metrics, process output and file references.

Start with the official Hyperparameter search example used in this tutorial. Its six activities prepare a dataset, run three training trials, compare their measured errors and register the best model.

The catalog also includes astronomical image mosaicking, OpenOil ensembles, model conversion, RAG pipelines, agent workflows, document processing and rendering. Browse by category or search for a workflow that matches your work. The Showcase connects examples to their source and supporting evidence.

Open full resolution ↗

AkôFlow Hub and Docker Hub have different jobs. AkôFlow Hub shares workflows and experiment evidence. Docker Hub supplies container images that activities can use. Workflows may also reference images from other registries; this tutorial's example uses an immutable image from GHCR.

Before you begin​

Use a current AkôFlow Desktop and daemon with the Hub controls shown below. You can browse public publications without signing in. Publishing requires a Hub account, a destination project and a finished local execution. Importing creates a local definition; running it also requires compatible infrastructure and access to the workflow's images and inputs.

These screenshots come from the live public Hub and a working local Desktop. The publishing walkthrough uses a new private tutorial publication. Its result was uploaded successfully, and the import walkthrough creates a separate local copy from that same private publication. Public Hub screenshots show the official example; the Desktop screenshots use our tutorial reference on the local Hub service. The GIFs replay captured steps; pause on any still image for the details. No new execution or infrastructure provisioning was started while recording.

Export a workflow as YAML​

  1. In Desktop, open Workflows → Definitions and select a workflow.
  2. Select Export YAML, the download action beside the workflow title.
  3. Save the .yaml file. This exports the portable definition, including its activities and dependencies.

Open full resolution ↗

A YAML export carries the definition. It does not package your execution history, local infrastructure or datasets. To share recorded results with the definition, use Publish to Hub below. To move just the file to another Desktop, select Import YAML in its workflow catalog.

Publish a finished execution to AkôFlow Hub​

1. Connect Desktop to your Hub project​

Open Settings → AkôFlow Hub and select Sign in to AkôFlow Hub. Continue in the browser, check the displayed authorization code, sign in and authorize the destination project. Desktop detects approval automatically.

When ready, the settings page shows Connected to AkôFlow Hub and the selected destination. You enter your Hub password in the browser, and the connection is scoped to the authorized project.

Open full resolution ↗

2. Open the result you want to share​

Open a finished execution and select Publish to Hub. This publishes a snapshot of that execution with the workflow version it actually used, even if you edited the definition afterward.

Open full resolution ↗

3. Choose or create a publication​

Choose an existing destination when you want to add evidence to the same publication. For a new workflow, select New publication, enter a title, review the generated slug and choose its visibility. Select Create publication to continue.

Publications start private. A public publication makes the selected content available to other people; choose that visibility when you intend to share it openly.

Open full resolution ↗

4. Select the evidence to include​

The workflow definition, scheduling context and execution summary are always included. Add a version message, then choose any optional sections:

OptionWhat it adds
Process logsRecorded output from activities.
File referencesRecorded file metadata and locations.
Activity metricsDetailed resource measurements collected during execution.
Execution eventsRecorded events and execution timeline.

All four options start unchecked. File references describe files; their contents are not uploaded by this publishing flow. Full datasets and binary artifacts stay outside the capture.

Open full resolution ↗

5. Review, then publish​

Select Review result. Inspect the destination, visibility, workflow YAML, version changes and any selected logs or file references. Review the content even when automatic redaction reports no secrets.

Open full resolution ↗

Select Publish reviewed result. Public destinations also require you to acknowledge making the capture public. Wait for Result published, then select Open publication in AkôFlow Hub to get its link.

Open full resolution ↗

The Hub keeps workflow versions immutable and attaches captured results to their version. A new execution can add evidence without requiring you to change the workflow definition.

Watch the export and publication steps

Open full resolution ↗

Import a published workflow into Desktop​

1. Choose a workflow version in the Hub​

Open a public publication and find Import into Desktop. Choose v1 for a fixed version, or Latest when you want the version that is newest at import time. Select Copy URI.

For the official example on the public Hub service, the fixed reference is:

akoflow::o/akoflow/machine-learning-hyperparameter-search:v1

The Desktop screenshots use akoflow::ovvesley/akoflow-hub-tutorial-hyperparameter-search:v1, our private demonstration copy. Copy a reference you can access from your own configured Hub service rather than typing the demonstration reference.

The o/akoflow part identifies the organization. Personal publications use the author's username instead. The final :v1 selects a workflow version; :latest resolves the latest available version. Record the resolved version when you need to repeat an experiment.

Open full resolution ↗

2. Load the definition in Desktop​

Open Workflows → Definitions → Create workflow, choose Import from Hub, paste the reference into Hub workflow URI and select Load definition.

Open full resolution ↗

3. Review the YAML and name your copy​

Check the resolved reference and version. Expand Preview workflow YAML to inspect the activities and commands. Desktop suggests a unique local name; keep it or enter your own.

Open full resolution ↗

Select Import workflow definition. Desktop opens the imported workflow, where you can inspect its graph and generate a plan.

Open full resolution ↗

Importing creates your own local definition. Execution history, environments and datasets remain at the source. It also leaves the author's publication unchanged.

Watch the import steps

Open full resolution ↗

Make the imported workflow runnable​

An imported graph is the starting point. Before selecting Generate plan, open the publication's README and Images & environment section to check its requirements.

For Hyperparameter search:

  1. Open the example source directory and follow its local setup instructions.
  2. Make the declared executable image available to your runtime. Preserve its immutable digest when reproducing the published capture.
  3. Register the companion environment.yaml, scope.yaml and topology.yaml in the order documented by the example. Check that the environment's resource, runtime and workspace paths match your machine.
  4. In Desktop, open the imported workflow, select Generate plan, choose the prepared execution scope and run HEFT. Review a feasible candidate.
  5. Select Execute plan, confirm Real execution, and follow the run until it completes. Check the activity outcomes and generated files before publishing your result.

For an introduction to local execution, follow From a DAG to your first run. Your timing and outputs should be assessed against your own inputs and environment; a published result is a record of its original run.

Where Docker Hub fits​

When building or adapting an activity, open Choose an artifact → Import from Docker Hub. Search for a public repository, choose a tag and a compatible Linux architecture, then review the artifact ID and version. The import registers the artifact and builds its Apptainer SIF. Wait for verification before selecting it in the activity; monitor its artifact page if the build fails.

Open full resolution ↗

Docker/OCI and SIF/Apptainer execution depend on the target environment. Choose an image that contains the tools your activity command needs. Replacing this example's GHCR image with a generic Python image would omit its packaged application code.

If a step does not work​

What you seeWhat to check
Hub is not configuredAsk the installation operator to configure the Hub service, then reopen Hub settings.
Cannot publishConnect the project in Hub settings and use a finished execution in a writable instance.
Reference cannot be loadedCopy the URI again, verify the owner and version, and check access to private content and the installation's configured Hub service.
Local name already existsAccept Desktop's suggested alternative or choose another name.
Review expired or destination changedReturn to the selection step and request a fresh review.
Imported workflow has no feasible planCheck the companion environment, execution scope, resources, images and workspace configuration.

Explore AkôFlow Hub, import a version that interests you, and publish the evidence from your own run. The next person can start from your workflow and see how you reached the result.

item.title: AkôFlow 1.0.14 — global search, audit and infrastructure navigation
item.description: Search control-plane records, explore API and runtime audit, discover keyboard shortcuts and inspect infrastructure by ownership.
item.content:encoded:
AkôFlow 1.0.14 adds fast global search, a keyboard shortcut reference, comprehensive audit exploration and a resource-oriented infrastructure map. These changes build on 1.0.13.

Database compatibility: this release consolidates the current schema into one canonical bootstrap. Existing databases with older schema checksums are not migrated in place. Preserve a verified backup and the previous installation before switching; use a new empty database for the new writable installation. The application does not silently reset incompatible databases. Request history is stored in a separate request-audit.db sidecar and must be backed up separately when needed.

The screenshots show the actual release candidate. Audit and settings use the local installation; search and infrastructure use existing experiments opened by a separate daemon in read-only archive mode. Capturing these images did not start workflow execution, provisioning or connectivity checks. Capture provenance is stored alongside the images.

Explore recorded activity in Audit​

Use the event timeline, server-side counts, outcome and transport facets, configurable time ranges, grouped results and cursor pagination to investigate API access, MCP protocol activity and runtime lifecycle events. Access records include authentication outcome, request and correlation identifiers, method, status and duration. Shared tokens identify service clients, not invented human identities.

Open full resolution ↗

Search and combine audit filters​

Search available filter choices, inspect recorded counts and combine filters to narrow an investigation. Additional references include request/correlation identifiers, executions, activities and operations. Loading, empty, retry and outdated-daemon states are explicit.

Open full resolution ↗

Inspect request and identity evidence​

Open an event in the shared full-height detail drawer without leaving the current results. Request, identity, target and correlation evidence stays together, with links to related records. Escape closes the drawer and restores focus. Bodies, authorization headers and secret values are not collected as audit payloads.

Open full resolution ↗

Follow completed HTTP requests​

The API requests view lists completed calls with method, path, status, duration, direct peer IP and caller classification. Fetch 50 records per page, navigate with cursors and refresh to return to the newest entries. Long-lived requests appear after completion. Query strings, bodies, cookies and authorization headers are omitted; caller-supplied client labels are not verified identity.

Open full resolution ↗

Configure request retention​

Settings exposes request-log retention from 1 to 3650 days, with a default of 30 days. Bounded periodic cleanup removes expired request records; operational audit events are preserved separately. Reducing retention can permanently remove older request records.

Open full resolution ↗

Discover shortcuts and their controls​

Open Settings → Keyboard shortcuts, or use the shortcut icon in the top bar. The reference shows macOS and Windows/Linux combinations, where each shortcut applies and its matching button or control. Try global search directly from the reference. Contextual keys cover search results, audit menus, activity dependencies and detail panels.

Open full resolution ↗

Find records with global search​

Press Command/Ctrl+K or use the top-bar search field to find workflows, executions, environments and artifacts by ID or partial name. Resources, plans, execution scopes and materializations are also searchable. Results show type, version, status and owner context; owner and result links are independently clickable.

The daemon reads bounded metadata projections instead of loading complete catalogs, logs or workflow definitions. Results use stable cursor pagination; the interface debounces typing, cancels obsolete requests and rejects stale responses. Keyboard navigation and mobile access are supported. A local Apple M4 Pro benchmark with 100,000 execution records measured approximately 73–120 ms per search; this is a local benchmark, not a universal latency guarantee.

Open full resolution ↗

Navigate infrastructure by ownership​

The environment map uses a vertical ownership tree with separate local, cloud and simulation branches when configured. Resources and network links have explicit entry points. Simulation adapters without bound resources do not create empty branches, and Fit view helps navigate the graph. Availability observations remain separate from configuration.

Open full resolution ↗

Inspect resources in the shared drawer​

Inspect resources and their recorded metadata in the shared full-height drawer, preserving opening/closing animations, focus handling and Escape dismissal. Search large resource lists and expand large HPC branches incrementally. Resource actions open their owning pages; on writable connected instances, available console actions hand sessions to the standard console bar instead of creating competing terminal views.

Open full resolution ↗

Read configured network links​

Inspect configured bandwidth, latency and link metadata from the environment map. Optional animated flow respects motion preferences. Diagram arrows illustrate configured relationships, not measured live traffic. The screenshot shows archived simulation configuration.

Open full resolution ↗

Find resources without expanding every branch​

The resource entry point opens a searchable side list. Filter recorded resources and inspect an item without losing the environment map. Available console actions on writable connected resources use the standard console bar.

Open full resolution ↗

Keep large HPC environments readable​

Large HPC branches initially show a small set of nodes and an explicit remaining count. Expand incrementally while keeping the full recorded inventory searchable. This archived environment contains 132 resources.

Open full resolution ↗

Keep the same tools in dark mode​

Audit timelines, facets, filter menus and shared drawers use the current appearance settings in both light and dark themes.

Open full resolution ↗

Other improvements​

  • Workflow command fields show shell highlighting and syntax-validation state. Daemon syntax validation checks scripts without executing them.
  • Environment editing preserves persisted identities, saved configuration and unbound resources.
  • Audit drawers retain the shared wrapper through closing animations, and older daemon responses display actionable update guidance.
  • The database's complete initial schema now includes scheduler-plugin tables; startup no longer applies the former incremental schema migrations.
  • Global search remains available for read-only imported archives and follows the selected instance's data.

Install and update​

Get the 1.0.14 release packages or follow the installation guide. Desktop packages support macOS universal, Windows x64 and Linux x64. Matching daemon and BuildKit archives support Linux amd64 and arm64. Docker Desktop is required on macOS/Windows; Linux requires Docker Engine and Compose v2.

Read the database compatibility note above before updating an existing installation. Runtime archives are loaded locally by Desktop; no container-registry deployment is required.

Validation​

  • Daemon: complete Go suite, architecture checks and go vet passed.
  • Desktop: 118 unit tests, 20 packaging/MCP/appearance contract tests, dependency-security checks, formatting and production build passed.
  • Browser: 86 development checks passed, with one production-only check skipped; 46 selected production checks passed, including the shortcuts screen in both themes.
  • Global search: matching, owner navigation, pagination, invalid cursors, cancellation, stale responses and a 100,000-record benchmark were checked.
  • Screenshot capture: 13 actual-interface images with capture provenance and no workload execution.

Frozen source tags: daemon and documentation and Desktop. Full release tour.

item.title: AkôFlow 1.0.13 — workflow monitoring, files, logs and temporal events
item.description: Explore workflow outputs by producer, read complete and activity logs, and inspect temporal execution events.
item.content:encoded:
AkôFlow 1.0.13 reorganizes execution monitoring around the workflow, its activities and the files they produce. This page describes changes since 1.0.12.

The screenshots below show the release candidate interface reading an existing completed six-activity Python workflow. Capturing them did not start a new execution. They demonstrate recorded observations, not a live filesystem listing. Capture provenance is stored alongside the images.

Workflow overview​

Follow the workflow as a whole: preparation artifacts, execution environments, recorded results and the execution plan. The unused external-input card has been removed.

Open full resolution ↗

Files next to their producer​

Workspace now connects activities to generated file nodes. Each activity previews its five largest files; the “…” node opens the complete list. Search activities or file paths in the explorer and click a result to focus the DAG. All, Path to activity, Branch, Fit view and fullscreen help navigate larger graphs.

Open full resolution ↗

Plan versus execution​

Compare planned and observed duration and cost, including absolute and relative differences. Activity counts and configured deadline/budget constraints remain explicit. Unconfigured constraints are not presented as satisfied SLAs. The Gantt charts retain their existing layout.

Open full resolution ↗

Search activities while reading logs​

A searchable activity explorer focuses the log DAG. The main log remains the complete run output.

Open full resolution ↗

Complete run logs​

Search messages and sources, navigate matches, wrap lines, follow new output, copy visible output, download logs or use fullscreen. Raw output without recorded timestamps is not given invented timestamps.

Open full resolution ↗

Activity logs in a drawer​

Click an activity to open its log in a side drawer without replacing the complete run log. View activity opens its execution details.

Open full resolution ↗

Activity details​

The activity drawer includes execution placement, timing, preparation and generated files, with a link to the owned activity page.

Open full resolution ↗

Preparation belongs to the activity​

Preparation is collapsible and updates during execution, with waiting, preparing, ready and failure states. Copy log reports clipboard success or failure. The separate run-wide Prerequisites tab has been removed.

Open full resolution ↗

Generated files in activity details​

Both the activity page and drawer reuse the Workspace file component, filtered by producer. Inspect size, checksum and recorded locations. Deleted manifest entries are excluded; recorded locations may no longer exist after workspace cleanup.

Open full resolution ↗

Temporal events​

Workflow and activity lanes place events at recorded times. Event types use distinct marker shapes, and search/type filters narrow the view. Use the selector for overlapping or untimed events and download the complete available event collection as JSON.

Open full resolution ↗

Event details and phase observations​

Click a marker to inspect its data in a side drawer. Reconstructed timing observations carry an explicit source, duration and recorded timestamps; they are derived observations, not additional persisted audit events.

Open full resolution ↗

Timing totals with explanations​

Execution-time decomposition keeps aggregate totals and explains each phase. The duplicate per-activity phase table has moved into Events. Accumulated work can exceed elapsed wall time because activities overlap.

Open full resolution ↗

Appearance and readability​

Desktop is the default interface style, with Simple available in Settings. Neutral actions, opaque surfaces, compact navigation and corrected selected-item contrast improve light/dark readability. Desktop appearance preferences survive local-server port changes and application restarts.

Open full resolution ↗

Other changes since 1.0.12​

  • Workflow shell commands can be checked for POSIX shell syntax through the daemon validation endpoint before execution. Validation does not execute the command.
  • MCP activation no longer requires a detected native AI client; manual connection configuration remains available. MCP itself was introduced in 1.0.12.
  • Research tooling is archived outside runtime packages, and downloadable scheduling snippets are isolated from daemon packages.
  • Documentation now includes the MCP hands-on workflow tutorial and generated public release history.

Install and update​

Get the 1.0.13 release packages or follow the installation guide. Desktop packages are available for macOS universal, Windows x64 and Linux x64. Matching daemon and BuildKit runtime archives support Linux amd64 and arm64. Docker remains required.

See execution monitoring for the updated navigation and interpretation of timing observations.

item.title: AkôFlow 1.0.12 brings MCP to Claude and Codex
item.description: AkôFlow 1.0.12 introduces MCP integration. Connect Claude or Codex to create, execute and inspect scientific workflows, with a hands-on example.
item.content:encoded:
Starting with version 1.0.12, AkôFlow includes MCP integration to connect AI apps such as Claude and Codex directly to its workflow engine. You can now describe an experiment in a conversation and ask your assistant to create workflow definitions, prepare execution plans, start runs and inspect their results through AkôFlow tools.

MCP—Model Context Protocol—provides that connection. The assistant works with the same persisted definitions, plans and runs that you see in Desktop, using the permissions you grant to its connection. The 1.0.12 release brings managed app connections, native client setup, connection verification, credential rotation and revocation.

This tutorial takes that connection from setup to a result you can inspect: three activities turn the measurements 2, 4 and 6 into a report containing Mean: 4.00. You will connect your AI app, give it focused prompts, inspect the saved DAG, and execute the workflow on a local Docker runtime.

What you need​

  • AkôFlow Desktop and its matching runtime, open and showing Connected.
  • Docker running on the machine that executes the activities.
  • A local Codex client, Claude Code, or a supported Claude Desktop installation.
  • An internet connection for the first BusyBox image download.

The setup screenshots below come from real, isolated homeserver Desktop captures. The 1.0.12 setup verifies the complete administration catalog; this tutorial only needs Operate workflows. Your connection paths, tool count and instance names will differ. The workflow and execution screenshots show the separate homeserver demonstration made for this post.

The native setup and connector were tested with real MCP clients. These are AkôFlow screenshots, not screenshots of an authenticated Claude or Codex conversation. The prompts are instructions for you to run in your own AI app; wording and approval dialogs can vary between clients.

1. Enable MCP and choose an app​

Open Settings → MCP & AI apps, then select Enable MCP.

Open full resolution ↗

Select Add app, choose your client and give the connection a recognizable name, such as Codex — workflow learning. Select Operate workflows, then Create connection.

Open full resolution ↗

The reference screenshot has Full administration selected to verify its complete catalog. For this walkthrough, select Operate workflows instead. Read only can inspect records but cannot create the workflow. Create a separate connection for each AI app so you can revoke one independently.

2. Install the generated client configuration​

AkôFlow generates a local stdio connection. The AI app starts the bundled connector on the same computer as Desktop. Keep Desktop open while using it.

Open full resolution ↗

Use the entry generated by your installation. The executable, helper and private connection-file paths in these screenshots belong to the documentation machine. Do not copy those paths into your own configuration.

Codex​

  1. Select Add to Codex in the setup dialog.
  2. Fully quit and reopen the app, then start a new local chat. For Codex CLI, start a new session.
  3. In the CLI, use /mcp to check active servers. codex mcp list lists configured servers.

AkôFlow writes its entry into the local Codex configuration, preserving other servers. If you use a custom configuration location, use Copy configuration or Open config to merge the generated entry into the configuration your client actually loads. Codex supports local stdio servers through config.toml; see the official Codex MCP documentation.

Claude Code​

  1. Choose Claude Code when creating the connection.
  2. Select Add to Claude Code in its setup dialog.
  3. Close the current Claude Code session and start a new one on this computer.
  4. Use /mcp to inspect the connection.

AkôFlow installs a user-level stdio entry in ~/.claude.json, preserving existing settings. For custom setups, use the generated entry and the official Claude Code MCP guide.

Claude Desktop​

On macOS or Windows, choose Claude Desktop and select Add to Claude Desktop. For manual setup, use Copy configuration, open Settings → Developer → Edit Config in Claude Desktop, and merge the generated server into mcpServers. Preserve other entries. Fully quit and reopen Claude Desktop, then begin a new conversation.

Open full resolution ↗

This Linux reference capture shows the copy-only fallback. Use the installation method that your AkôFlow setup dialog offers. The local MCP setup guide explains Claude Desktop's configuration and restart flow.

3. Verify both ends of the connection​

In AkôFlow, select Test MCP connection. A successful test authenticates a real MCP client, discovers the tools permitted for this connection, and reads the daemon identity.

Open full resolution ↗

Now send this prompt in your AI app:

Use the AkôFlow MCP tools to identify my connected AkôFlow instance
and list my workflows and available environments. If a list is empty,
tell me. Do not create or modify anything.

Checkpoint: the assistant makes an AkôFlow tool call and returns records from your instance, or an explicit empty list. An answer saying “I can help with AkôFlow” does not verify the connection. If it has no tools, reconnect its MCP server or restart the AI app.

The native test verifies the service. This first request verifies that your AI app loaded the server.

4. Ask for a concrete workflow​

Start with a small experiment whose answer you know. Send:

Use AkôFlow MCP to create a workflow named mcp-first-analysis in
namespace learning. First check whether that name already exists;
if it does, show it and do not overwrite it.

Use docker.io/library/busybox:1.36 with OCI delivery and sh -c.
Create three activities, each limited to 0.1 CPU and 32Mi memory:

1. prepare: write the values 2, 4 and 6, one per line, to measurements.txt.
2. analyze: depend on prepare, read measurements.txt, and use awk to
   write the arithmetic mean with two decimal places to mean.txt.
3. write-report: depend on analyze and write Mean: 4.00 to report.txt,
   deriving the value from mean.txt rather than hardcoding the answer.

Print each activity's output in its log and declare its output file
in expectedOutputs. Show the definition, create it through the MCP
tool, then read it back and return its workflow and version IDs.
Do not create a plan or start execution yet.
ActivityDepends onOutput
prepare—measurements.txt: 2, 4, 6
analyzepreparemean.txt: 4.00
write-reportanalyzereport.txt: Mean: 4.00

Open Workflows → Definitions → mcp-first-analysis in Desktop. The saved workflow must have three activities and two dependency arrows.

Open full resolution ↗

Checkpoint: compare the saved definition with the table. A chat response containing YAML is only a draft until the creation tool succeeds and readback confirms the record. Creating the definition does not execute it.

For an exact reference, download the complete workflow YAML. It uses command.executable.source for the container image, dependsOn for ordering, and expectedOutputs for required files. AkôFlow stages a predecessor's workspace before its dependent activity starts. Each activity writes a different output filename.

5. Select where it will run​

If you have no local environment yet, follow Connect your local machine and create a scope. Test the connection before saving the environment and confirm it is online. An execution scope selects the environment versions offered to planning.

Ask the assistant to discover those records:

Use AkôFlow MCP to inspect mcp-first-analysis and list execution scopes,
their environments, resources, runtime bindings and connection health.
Find a scope with a healthy local execution runtime that supports OCI
containers. Return the exact persisted IDs and explain the selection.
Do not provision cloud resources or execute anything. If no suitable
scope exists, tell me what I need to configure in Desktop.

Then request the plan, replacing the bracketed text with the scope you reviewed:

Create a manual plan for the saved version of mcp-first-analysis using
[my reviewed local scope]. Resolve IDs from the persisted records.
Assign all three activities to its local resource and execution runtime.
Use one second per activity as a planning estimate, preserve dependency
order, and save the plan through MCP. Read it back and return its ID,
assignments, runtime selection and execution mode. Do not execute yet.

Review the saved plan in Desktop. One second is an estimate, not a measured duration or timeout. The first image download may take longer. The homeserver demonstration used one local Docker resource; it did not allocate cloud machines or use simulation.

6. Execute once and wait for evidence​

When the plan matches your intent, send:

Start one real execution of the reviewed plan for mcp-first-analysis.
Use a unique run ID and return it as soon as submission succeeds.
Poll that run until it reaches a terminal state. Do not resubmit it
because it is pending or running. If it fails, inspect its activity
errors and report the cause before creating any replacement run.

Open Workflows → Definitions → mcp-first-analysis → Plans, open the selected plan, and open its execution. Wait for completed and 3/3 completed activities.

Open full resolution ↗

MCP submissions can return an operation or pending receipt before the work finishes. Submission success is not execution success. Keep the returned identifier and inspect that same operation or run instead of starting duplicates.

7. Read the result, not just the status​

Inspect the completed run using AkôFlow MCP. Report each activity's
status and exit code, inspect the final activity output and generated
files, and verify that report.txt contains Mean: 4.00. Include file
checksums when available and the workflow, plan and run IDs.
Distinguish files listed in metadata from file contents actually read.
If content cannot be retrieved, say so instead of inferring it.

In Desktop, open the run's Activities, select write-report, and open its activity detail page. Inspect Activity output and Generated files.

Open full resolution ↗

Follow the data through the workflow​

Open the run’s Workspaces & data tab. The activity/file graph connects each producer to its recorded output: prepare produces measurements.txt, analyze produces mean.txt, and write-report produces report.txt.

Open full resolution ↗

Open prepare and scroll to Activity output to check the actual input values. The log prints 2, 4 and 6; the generated-file record identifies measurements.txt and its checksum.

Open full resolution ↗

Open analyze to inspect the intermediate result. Its output is 4.00, and its generated file is mean.txt.

Open full resolution ↗

Back in Workspaces & data, scroll to the recorded file locations and Data transfers. The demonstration records two workspace transfers totaling 17 bytes. These transfers stage predecessor workspaces, so the second transfer includes the intermediate workspace’s files; its byte count is not just the size of mean.txt. Recorded locations describe execution evidence and may become unavailable after ephemeral workspaces are released.

Open full resolution ↗

The demonstration created mcp-first-analysis, saved mcp-analysis-plan, and executed mcp-analysis-run. The real run completed all three activities. Reading the final workspace file confirmed:

Mean: 4.00

The workflow creation, planning, submission and status retrieval went through a real stdio MCP client on the homeserver. The final file contents were additionally checked directly in the isolated runtime workspace. Download the observed verification record.

More prompts to try​

Change one aspect at a time so you can explain the result.

A new dataset:

Create a new workflow named mcp-analysis-10-20-30 using the same
three-stage structure, but with values 10, 20 and 30. Preserve the
original workflow. Show the changed commands and expected answer
before saving the new definition. Do not execute yet.

Independent branches:

Draft a workflow that prepares measurements, computes the mean and
maximum in independent activities, then joins both into one report.
Show its DAG and file handoffs. Add dependencies only where a stage
needs its predecessor's files, and use distinct output filenames.
Explain whether my selected resource capacity permits parallel work.
Do not save or execute until I review the draft.

Investigate a failure:

Inspect run [run ID] through AkôFlow MCP. Find the first failing
activity, quote the relevant error briefly, and distinguish an image,
connection, planning or command failure. Propose the smallest fix.
Do not change infrastructure or retry the run yet.

Prepare a reproducibility summary:

Summarize run [run ID] using persisted AkôFlow records: workflow version,
container reference and resolved digest if recorded, scope, assignments,
activity outcomes, output paths and available checksums. Mark missing
evidence explicitly. Do not treat planned durations as measurements.

When a step does not work​

SymptomNext check
AkôFlow verifies MCP but the assistant has no toolsRestart the client, start a new local session, and inspect its active MCP servers.
The assistant can list records but cannot create themRecreate its connection with Operate workflows.
Configuration points to another computer or an old application pathGenerate it again from the Desktop installation on the client machine.
No healthy local runtime appearsTest the environment connection and inspect its resource/runtime binding.
A run is pendingInspect its operation and run events; keep polling the same ID.
The first activity cannot startInspect its error and Docker/image availability before retrying.
analyze cannot find measurements.txtCheck the dependency, predecessor outcome and workspace-staging evidence.
The run completes but the answer differsRead the saved commands and actual files; verify the input values and formatting.

Use Disable MCP to pause connections, Rotate credential to replace a connection's credential, or Revoke access to remove one app's access. Reconnect the AI app after rotation. Keep secret values out of prompts and use the generated private references.

You now have a reusable pattern: describe a checkable experiment, save and inspect its definition, select a compatible execution scope, review a plan, execute once, and inspect the evidence. Continue with workflow authoring, planning, and the MCP setup and permissions guide.

item.title: From a DAG to your first AkôFlow run
item.description: With AkôFlow Desktop installed, follow annotated screenshots to create your first local workflow, execute it, and inspect its output.
item.content:encoded:
With AkôFlow Desktop already installed, your first experiment can start on your own workstation. Describe one activity in YAML, select your local machine, and watch a real execution produce a file. Then turn that first activity into a small analysis pipeline.

This walkthrough uses AkôFlow Desktop throughout. Desktop starts its matching local services and manages the connection to the engine. You do not need to clone the source repository, start a development Compose stack, or copy an API token.

What you will build​

Begin with write-report: one activity that writes result.txt and prints its contents in the activity log. This checks the complete path from a definition to a local execution and its recorded output.

After that succeeds, import a second YAML with three activities: prepare three measurements, compute their mean, and write a report. The expected answer is 4.00.

Both examples use a small BusyBox container on your local Docker engine. They perform real execution. They do not simulate work or allocate cloud machines.

1. Begin after Desktop is installed​

This walkthrough starts after installing AkôFlow Desktop. If you still need the application, follow Install AkôFlow Desktop, then return here.

  1. Start Docker and open the installed AkôFlow Desktop application.
  2. Let the engine checkup finish and wait for Overview.
  3. Confirm Connected at the bottom-left corner.
  4. Start with Infrastructure → Environments in the sidebar.

The screenshots below were captured from the actual interface. They show the controls using an existing reference instance: its workflow is named hello, its activity is a, and its local environment is Local environment. For your experiment, enter the tutorial names first-local-check, write-report, Local check, and First local scope. Your fresh catalogs may be empty. The reference run's counts and files are identified in each caption rather than presented as your experiment's results.

Each red number has a matching instruction below the image. Click a screenshot to enlarge it with its arrows; on a phone, scroll the enlarged view sideways to read the controls.

Checkpoint: Desktop is connected. If startup fails, open its failure details before retrying.

2. Connect your local machine​

Open Infrastructure → Environments. To create the environment from scratch, follow the two screens below. If you already created Local check, open it and continue with its connection check instead.

  1. Select Connect environment (called New environment in some releases), then Local machine.
  2. Name it Local check.
  3. Select Test connection.
  4. When the test succeeds, select Save environment.

On the environment page, select Check now. Wait until Local machine shows online. This makes the local resource available for planning.

An environment describes where the work can run. Here, the target is the machine reached through your local AkôFlow engine. Desktop requests connection checks from the daemon.

Checkpoint: the local resource is online. Remember its environment name for step 5.

3. Save your first workflow YAML​

Create a plain-text file named first-local-check.yaml, or download the complete YAML. Copy the whole document, preserving indentation, and save it with the .yaml extension.

name: first-local-check
spec:
  namespace: learning
  activities:
    - name: write-report
      cpuLimit: "0.1"
      memoryLimit: 32Mi
      command:
        executable:
          source:
            type: oci
            reference: docker.io/library/busybox:1.36
          delivery:
            strategy: auto
            targetFormat: oci
        entrypoint: sh
        arguments:
          - -c
          - |
            printf 'Akoflow local check\n' > result.txt
            cat result.txt
      expectedOutputs: [result.txt]

Read the document from the outside in:

  • name identifies the workflow. namespace groups it under learning.
  • activities contains one unit of work: write-report.
  • command.executable names the BusyBox image. targetFormat: oci selects the container format used by local Docker.
  • entrypoint: sh and the -c argument run the following shell script.
  • printf creates the file in the activity workspace. cat prints it into the activity log.
  • expectedOutputs asserts that result.txt exists after execution.
  • CPU and memory limits describe the activity's small resource demand.

The image comes from Docker Hub, so its first use may take longer while it downloads. For a research reproducibility bundle, also retain the resolved image digest alongside the version tag.

4. Import the YAML in Desktop​

  1. Open Workflows → Definitions.
  2. Select Import YAML and choose first-local-check.yaml.
  3. Open the new first-local-check definition.
  4. Confirm that the DAG contains one activity named write-report.

A DAG is a directed acyclic graph: nodes are activities and arrows are dependencies. This first graph has one node and no arrows, enough to learn the execution lifecycle before adding data handoffs.

If the name already exists, open the existing definition or change name before importing another copy. The importer normalizes names into identifiers, so each new definition needs a distinct name.

Checkpoint: the definition exists and its graph matches the YAML. Importing saves a definition; it does not start a run.

5. Create a local execution scope​

  1. Open Infrastructure → Execution scopes.
  2. Select Create scope (called New execution scope in some releases).
  3. Name it First local scope and select your local environment.
  4. Leave Create the initial network topology enabled.
  5. Select Create execution scope.

After selecting Local check, scroll to the bottom of the form to save it:

A scope selects the environment resources offered to planning. Its topology describes the connections between them. A one-machine experiment needs no network links.

Desktop creates these records and their identifiers. The YAML here describes the workflow; you do not need to author environment, scope, or plan API envelopes.

6. Make a plan and start the run​

Return to first-local-check and select Generate plan:

  1. Choose Create manually.
  2. Select First local scope.
  3. Select write-report in the activity graph.
  4. Choose your local machine runtime and local machine resource.
  5. Set Expected execution time to 1 second.
  6. Select Generate plan.

The duration is an estimate, not a timeout or a measurement. Image download and startup can make the first run take longer.

On the saved plan page, select Execute plan:

Review the selected plan, Real execution, and the local runtime. Keep the suggested unique run ID or enter your own:

Scroll to the bottom, then select Start execution once:

Wait until the run says completed and 1/1 activities settled:

A plan describes where work should run. A run records what happened. Submission is asynchronous: pending or running can appear before completed.

7. Inspect your first result​

On the completed run, select Activities, then write-report. Open its Details link or Open activity page from its information panel (some releases label this Open activity details).

Where to lookExpected result
Execution detailsExit code 0
Activity output/logAkoflow local check
Generated filesresult.txt, with a SHA-256 checksum

Scroll down the activity page to Activity output and Generated files:

The generated file belongs to the activity workspace managed by the engine. Listing a file records that it was observed; it does not automatically download it into your computer's Downloads folder.

You have now submitted and inspected a real local experiment. Save the YAML with your experiment material so the definition can be reused.

8. Extend it into a small analysis​

Save the next document as first-local-analysis.yaml, or download the complete analysis YAML. This is a new, complete workflow, with a different name from the first definition.

ActivityReadsProduces
prepareValues declared in its command: 2, 4, 6measurements.txt
analyzemeasurements.txtmean.txt, containing 4.00
write-reportmean.txtreport.txt, containing Mean: 4.00
name: first-local-analysis
spec:
  namespace: learning
  activities:
    - name: prepare
      cpuLimit: "0.1"
      memoryLimit: 32Mi
      command:
        executable:
          source:
            type: oci
            reference: docker.io/library/busybox:1.36
          delivery:
            strategy: auto
            targetFormat: oci
        entrypoint: sh
        arguments:
          - -c
          - |
            printf '2\n4\n6\n' > measurements.txt
            cat measurements.txt
      expectedOutputs: [measurements.txt]

    - name: analyze
      dependsOn: [prepare]
      cpuLimit: "0.1"
      memoryLimit: 32Mi
      command:
        executable:
          source:
            type: oci
            reference: docker.io/library/busybox:1.36
          delivery:
            strategy: auto
            targetFormat: oci
        entrypoint: sh
        arguments:
          - -c
          - |
            awk '{sum += $1; n++} END {printf "%.2f\n", sum/n}' measurements.txt > mean.txt
            cat mean.txt
      expectedOutputs: [mean.txt]

    - name: write-report
      dependsOn: [analyze]
      cpuLimit: "0.1"
      memoryLimit: 32Mi
      command:
        executable:
          source:
            type: oci
            reference: docker.io/library/busybox:1.36
          delivery:
            strategy: auto
            targetFormat: oci
        entrypoint: sh
        arguments:
          - -c
          - |
            printf 'Mean: %s\n' "$(cat mean.txt)" > report.txt
            cat report.txt
      expectedOutputs: [report.txt]

The new field is dependsOn. analyze waits for prepare, and write-report waits for analyze. AkôFlow stages the predecessor's workspace before a dependent activity starts. Each stage writes a different output path, avoiding conflicting contents at the same path. expectedOutputs verifies that the required file exists.

Repeat the Desktop sequence:

  1. Import first-local-analysis.yaml in Workflows → Definitions.
  2. Confirm the three-node DAG above.
  3. Create a manual plan using the existing First local scope.
  4. Assign all three activities to the local runtime and resource, with an expected duration of 1 second each.
  5. Generate the plan, choose Execute plan → Real execution, and start it.
  6. Wait for completed and 3/3 activities settled.
  7. Open the final write-report activity. Its log should print Mean: 4.00. Its generated files should include report.txt with a checksum.

This graph is sequential because each stage consumes the previous stage's output. A future independent branch should declare only the dependencies it needs. Dependencies determine readiness; resource capacity determines whether ready activities can run together.

If something stops you​

SymptomNext action
Desktop does not reach ConnectedCheck Docker and inspect first-start failure details.
Local environment is offline or missing from planningTest its connection, save it, and select Check now.
YAML import failsCheck indentation, retain the complete name/spec wrapper, and use a distinct workflow name.
No compatible runtime appearsRecheck the environment's runtime binding and select a real local scope.
The first activity cannot obtain its imageInspect the activity error and verify access to Docker Hub and the local Docker engine.
Analysis cannot find its inputCheck dependsOn, the predecessor's completion, and workspace-staging evidence.
A run fails or stays pendingOpen activity details and run events, then see Troubleshooting.

The idea behind AkôFlow​

The original AkôFlow paper introduces middleware for parallel scientific workflows in containerized environments, with provenance capture and an astronomy evaluation. It gives the research context for the project:

Ferreira, W.; Kunstmann, L.; Paes, A.; Bedo, M.; de Oliveira, D. AkôFlow: um Middleware para execução de Workflows científicos em múltiplos ambientes conteinerizados. SBBD, 2024, pp. 27–39. Read the paper.

This post follows the current Desktop interface and portable workflow format, which have evolved since the publication. The paper explains the research motivation; the documentation and downloadable YAML files describe the steps used here.

Here, the YAML is the workflow definition, the environment is your local machine, the scope selects eligible resources, the plan assigns activities, and the run holds observed results. Generated files and checksums provide a first piece of execution evidence.

For your next experiment, change the measurements in a new copy of the analysis YAML and check that the mean changes accordingly. Continue with planning alternatives, workflow authoring, or the Montage 050 scientific workflow.

API automation is a separate next step once you know these objects; see API access. The Desktop path manages its internal credentials for you.

item.title: Montage 050: a sky made of workflows
item.description: Twelve observations, 58 activities, one astronomical mosaic. Explore the science, reproduce the local workflow, and read the evidence behind a completed experiment.
item.content:encoded:
The stars in the opening image are the output of a scientific computation. Before the color mosaic existed, individual observations had to be reprojected, their overlaps compared, their backgrounds reconciled, and their pixels combined. AkôFlow coordinates those steps as a workflow and keeps the execution evidence alongside the result.

This field note follows Montage 050, a 58-activity astronomy workflow. We will look at what the activities do, how to reproduce the local example, and what an existing completed experiment tells us about planning and execution.

Start with the image—and its provenance​

The cover is the actual 1800 × 1800 color preview from run montage-docker-image-real-20261010-v2. It is a recorded product of a completed hybrid GCP/HPC experiment. Click it to enlarge the image, or open the original PNG.

That experiment and the local reproduction described below use different execution environments. The cover and historical timings establish what the completed hybrid run produced; they are not a claim that the two-slot local example finished in the same time.

The preserved PNG is 4,920,451 bytes. Its SHA-256 is:

63fa4d8447274bdb8a44f6be8cf5a23c0a2f0baa479bd2ae1ec3b541df4e19f2

The image copied into this site matches that checksum. You can download the observed result summary to connect the picture to the run, activity counts, timings, and audit checks.

What Montage does for astronomy​

A sky survey records many images rather than a single photograph of an entire region. Those images may use different pixel grids and have different background levels. Simply placing them next to each other would leave misalignment and visible seams.

Montage, developed at IPAC, combines astronomical images while preserving positional and calibration fidelity. Its building blocks operate on FITS files, the scientific image products in this workflow. The color PNG is a visualization of the resulting mosaics; retain the FITS products for scientific analysis.

Three operations explain much of the computation:

  • Reprojection: map observations onto a common output grid. The mProject documentation describes the input image, header template, reprojected image, and accompanying area image.
  • Background matching: measure overlap differences and solve for consistent corrections. mBgModel uses the fitted differences to estimate a global set of adjustments.
  • Coaddition: combine corrected observations into mosaics. The Montage module guide describes the tools for metadata generation, reprojection, background correction, and mosaicking.

Here, twelve input FITS observations feed three image-band branches. Each branch produces a FITS mosaic and a monochrome preview; a final activity combines the three mosaics into the color preview.

Which Montage example and which public data?​

This example is Montage 050, preserved in the original image as 050d. The identifier names the workload configuration; it does not mean that the graph contains 50 activities. Section 4.1 and Table 1 of the AkôFlow paper, SBBD 2024, describe the smaller “0.5” configuration with the same inventory used here: 12 projections, 18 overlap fits, and 58 activity executions in total. The paper also evaluates a larger “1.0” configuration with 472 executions. This walkthrough uses the smaller one. The bundled FITS header templates define its actual output footprint and pixel grid.

The inputs are real, publicly accessible astronomical survey images, rather than generated test pictures. Their names identify the POSS2/UKSTU survey products distributed through the Digitized Sky Survey (DSS) archive at IRSA. DSS digitizes photographic survey plates from the Palomar and UK Schmidt telescopes; IRSA provides image access and links to the originating STScI archive. The IRSA dataset summary documents that survey lineage. Public access does not remove the archive's attribution and copyright requirements; retain the DSS/STScI and original survey acknowledgments when reusing the images.

The pinned bundle contains four input tiles in each of three survey bands:

BranchSource filename familySource bandFITS mosaicDisplay channel in the final PNG
1poss2ukstu_blue_*.fitsBlue1-mosaic.fitsBlue
2poss2ukstu_red_*.fitsRed2-mosaic.fitsGreen
3poss2ukstu_ir_*.fitsNear infrared3-mosaic.fitsRed

That is 12 FITS inputs, approximately 87 MiB in the image's input seed. The RGB assignment is a visualization choice: the red survey band is displayed in green, and the infrared band in red. Read the scientific FITS products and their headers when interpreting measurements; PNG colors alone do not identify an observing wavelength.

The exact command and file inventory is available in the pinned workflow.yaml. Keeping that revision and the container digest identifies the packaged input set used for reproduction. Acquiring a fresh cutout from the public archive may select different pixels or preprocessing, so it is a new input set to record explicitly.

Inside the 58-activity graph​

The local bundle preserves the original commands, activity names, and 138 named file handoffs. Its activity inventory is:

Native commandActivitiesResponsibility
mProject12Reproject the input observations
mDiffFit18Compare overlaps and fit their differences
mConcatFit3Assemble fit results for each band
mBgModel3Solve each band's background corrections
mBackground12Apply corrections to the projected observations
mImgtbl3Build metadata tables for corrected images
mAdd3Coadd the three FITS mosaics
mViewer4Produce three monochrome previews and one color preview
Total58

The diagram below comes from the local example's activity and dependency contract. Enlarge it to follow individual edges.

Independent projections and overlap operations can run concurrently after their own inputs are ready. Background modeling introduces a convergence point within each band. The final color preview waits for its three mosaic inputs. There is no extra global barrier forcing an unrelated band to wait at every stage.

This is why the DAG matters: it encodes scientific dependencies. A scheduler can choose where ready work runs, but cannot skip an input merely to make the graph appear more parallel. The Montage parallelization guide explains the relationship between independent image operations and background-model convergence.

What each activity does, and what its parameters mean​

The scientific design follows Jacob et al., Montage: a grid portal and software toolkit for science-grade astronomical image mosaicking, especially its toolkit components and workflow discussion. Reprojection aligns the pixel grids; overlap fitting supplies evidence for background adjustments; corrected images are then coadded. The sections below combine that explanation with the module manuals and the actual arguments in this example.

An activity type, such as mProject, can have several executions in the graph. Here, the same processing chain repeats for three bands. The examples below show the first band unless noted otherwise. They run inside an activity workspace after AkôFlow has staged the declared inputs; copying one command into an empty directory is not a complete reproduction.

mProject: put one observation on the common sky grid​

mProject -X poss2ukstu_blue_001_001.fits pposs2ukstu_blue_001_001.fits region-oversized.hdr

Each of the 12 executions reprojects one observation. It maps input pixels through sky coordinates onto the requested output grid, accounting for pixel overlap rather than merely resizing a picture. Its outputs include the projected FITS image and an accompanying _area.fits coverage image.

ParameterMeaning in this example
-XExpand the template region as necessary to retain the input image's extent.
poss2ukstu_blue_001_001.fitsInput observation.
pposs2ukstu_blue_001_001.fitsProjected output; the p prefix is this workflow's naming convention.
region-oversized.hdrFITS header template defining the working grid, coordinate projection, reference coordinates, and pixel scale. It is used before the final mosaic footprint is applied.

These tasks have no predecessor activities and can start independently when execution slots are available. See the official mProject manual.

mDiffFit: measure how two projected images disagree​

mDiffFit -d -s 1-fit.000001.000002.txt pposs2ukstu_blue_001_001.fits pposs2ukstu_blue_001_002.fits 1-diff.000001.000002.fits region-oversized.hdr

The 18 executions compare overlapping pairs: six pairs among the four images in each band. mDiffFit combines image differencing (mDiff) with a plane fit (mFitplane). It measures relative background offsets and gradients that the next stages need.

ParameterMeaning in this example
-dEnable diagnostic output.
-s 1-fit.000001.000002.txtWrite the structured fit/status result for this pair to a named file.
The two pposs2ukstu_…fits argumentsProjected images to compare; both projection tasks must finish first.
1-diff.000001.000002.fitsDifference-image path used by the combined operation.
region-oversized.hdrShared working-grid template.

Different pairs can run concurrently after their respective inputs arrive. See the Montage grid-tool description and mDiffFit implementation and command interface.

mConcatFit: gather the pairwise measurements​

mConcatFit 1-stat.tbl 1-fits.tbl .

There are three executions, one per band. Each gathers the individual overlap-fit records into the table required by background modeling. It combines fit parameters, not image pixels.

ParameterMeaning in this example
1-stat.tblInput table identifying the fit-result files to collect.
1-fits.tblOutput table of pairwise fit measurements.
.Directory containing those staged fit-result files: the current workspace.

This task waits for the band's six mDiffFit executions. The grid-tool guide explains why independently generated fit records need this merge; the mConcatFit source documents its three positional arguments.

mBgModel: solve a consistent background model for the band​

mBgModel -i 100000 1-images.tbl 1-fits.tbl 1-corrections.tbl

The three executions use the overlap measurements together to find per-image background corrections. A global solution within each band avoids treating each seam as an unrelated adjustment. The result is a correction table; the image pixels are changed by the following activity.

ParameterMeaning in this example
-i 100000Iteration count requested by this versioned workload's modeling command; it is not a timeout or CPU allocation. Preserve it when reproducing the pinned example.
1-images.tblInput image metadata and identifiers.
1-fits.tblAggregated measurements from mConcatFit.
1-corrections.tblOutput coefficients for correcting each image's background.

This is a convergence point for each band. Other bands can progress independently. The official mBgModel manual explains the solver and its arguments; documented iteration limits can differ from the packaged command, so the pinned image remains the reference for this reproduction.

mBackground: apply the correction to one projected image​

mBackground -t pposs2ukstu_blue_001_001.fits cposs2ukstu_blue_001_001.fits 1-projected.tbl 1-corrections.tbl

Each of the 12 executions subtracts the fitted background plane from one projected image. In the module's model, the plane has the form A*x + B*y + C. This matches relative backgrounds while retaining the image for coaddition; it is not a command to remove every astronomical source or all diffuse emission.

ParameterMeaning in this example
-tTable mode: obtain the image's correction coefficients from the supplied tables rather than three explicit coefficient arguments.
pposs2ukstu_blue_001_001.fitsProjected input image.
cposs2ukstu_blue_001_001.fitsBackground-corrected output; c is the workflow's naming convention.
1-projected.tblMetadata table used to identify the projected image.
1-corrections.tblPer-image corrections produced by mBgModel.

Corrections for different images can run concurrently once their band model and projected inputs are ready. See the official mBackground manual.

mImgtbl: describe the corrected files for the coaddition step​

mImgtbl . -t 1-corrected.tbl 1-updated-corrected.tbl

The three executions read FITS headers and create metadata tables. Those tables describe image geometry and file identity so that coaddition can place the corrected inputs correctly. This stage produces metadata, not another mosaic.

ParameterMeaning in this example
.Directory in which to read the corrected FITS files.
-t 1-corrected.tblRestrict processing to the images named in this input list, rather than every FITS file in the workspace.
1-updated-corrected.tblOutput table with the corrected files' header metadata.

Each task waits for its band's four corrected images. The official mImgtbl manual documents the table fields and selection option.

mAdd: coadd the corrected observations into one FITS mosaic​

mAdd -e 1-updated-corrected.tbl region.hdr 1-mosaic.fits

The three executions create one scientific mosaic per band from the corrected, aligned images. Coaddition combines contributions where pixels overlap; it is not concatenation of files or an RGB operation. Montage also produces an area/coverage mosaic.

ParameterMeaning in this example
-eUse the exact dimensions in the final header template instead of shrinking the mosaic to the data's bounding region.
1-updated-corrected.tblMetadata table selecting the images to coadd.
region.hdrFinal mosaic template, as distinct from the oversized working template used earlier. The recorded output is 1800 × 1800 pixels.
1-mosaic.fitsOutput scientific mosaic for this band.

No averaging-mode override (-a) is supplied in this command. The official mAdd manual describes the coaddition modes and area-image behavior.

mViewer: turn scientific mosaics into viewable PNGs​

The first three executions render one preview per band:

mViewer -ct 1 -gray 1-mosaic.fits -1s max gaussian -png 1-mosaic.png
ParameterMeaning in this example
-ct 1Select color-table index 1 for the single-band display.
-gray 1-mosaic.fitsRead one FITS image for single-band rendering.
-1s maxSet the display range using a sigma-based lower bound and the maximum as the upper bound.
gaussianUse Gaussian histogram-based stretching for display.
-png 1-mosaic.pngWrite the rendered PNG.

The fourth execution builds the color preview after all three mAdd tasks finish:

mViewer -red 3-mosaic.fits -0.5s max gaussian-log -green 2-mosaic.fits -0.5s max gaussian-log -blue 1-mosaic.fits -0.5s max gaussian-log -png mosaic-color.png

Here, -red, -green, and -blue assign FITS mosaics to display channels. Each receives its own -0.5s max range and gaussian-log stretch. -png names the final output. These choices control visualization, not the calibrated FITS pixel values.

The official mViewer examples describe these interfaces. Berriman and Good's visualization paper explains the scientific visualization context. The three single-band previews and the color preview are sibling consumers of the FITS mosaics: the color task does not need to wait for the preview PNGs.

Scientific parameters and execution settings are different​

The command arguments above determine image processing and file products. The YAML also supplies AkôFlow settings such as cpuLimit: 1000m (one CPU), memoryLimit: 1Gi, the selected runtime, and dependsOn. Those govern execution placement, limits, and readiness; they are not flags passed to Montage. workspaceSeedPath identifies the packaged seed, while historical simulation.durationSeconds values support planning and do not measure a new real execution.

Reproduce the workload locally​

If this is your first AkôFlow experiment, begin with the Desktop walkthrough. It teaches definitions, environments, scopes, plans, and runs with a tiny local workload.

The full Montage bundle adds a command-line preparation and execution path. Have Git, Go 1.23 or newer, and Docker with linux/amd64 support available. Keep at least 15 GiB of free disk for the image and intermediate workspaces. Retention and concurrency affect the peak requirement. Apple Silicon runs this amd64 workload through emulation and may take substantially longer.

1. Get the versioned example​

git clone https://github.com/UFFeScience/akoflow-examples.git
cd akoflow-examples
git checkout --detach d890c3171e3661890305b763b8fc3ede48bb61b4
cd scientific-workflows/montage-050

Pinning the checkout makes this walkthrough refer to a specific example revision. The bundle README documents its requirements and commands.

The bundle contains workflow.yaml, environment.yaml, scope.yaml, and topology.yaml, plus preparation, execution, and validation scripts. The workflow retains historical simulation durations as model inputs. Use the provided runner or daemon helper for the real workload; importing that source YAML alone is not the complete real-execution setup.

2. Prepare the image and inputs​

./prepare.sh

Preparation obtains the pinned image and Go dependencies, and checks the command/input contract. The image includes approximately 87 MiB of source FITS data, region headers, lookup tables, and the native Montage tools. There is no need to locate twelve observations manually.

The upstream image is pinned by digest:

ovvesley/akoflow-wf-montage@sha256:26b060b83b990557ea86ab40503cc8f17ab6016b5973e7e6f9201100a96440c9

Preparation success establishes that the inputs and commands are available. It does not mean all scientific activities have executed.

3. Execute the complete local DAG​

./run.sh

The standalone runner uses two CPU slots by default. Each activity becomes eligible once its dependencies finish and a slot is available. It copies the bundled input seed, executes the native commands with network access disabled, and writes activity observations under outputs/.

This path provisions no cloud machines and needs no remote HPC account. It is a substantial scientific workload: allow it to finish rather than interpreting a slow projection as a completed run.

4. Validate and open the products​

./validate.sh

Inspect the final files in outputs/:

ProductWhat it gives you
1-mosaic.fits, 2-mosaic.fits, 3-mosaic.fitsThree 1800 × 1800 scientific mosaics
1-mosaic.png, 2-mosaic.png, 3-mosaic.pngMonochrome visual previews
mosaic-color.pngCombined color preview
manifest.jsonGenerated artifacts and SHA-256 digests
dag-validation.jsonDependency-wave validation
stage-<activity>.jsonPer-activity observations

The validator checks all 58 activity records, FITS dimensions, and PNG headers. A successful manifest is published only after the workflow and final-file checks pass. Merely finding one intermediate image is insufficient to declare the experiment complete.

Inspect a daemon-managed run in Desktop​

The bundle also supports a daemon helper that registers the local environment, builds the declared image, and submits the 58 activities to the engine. This advanced path requires a daemon whose API address and token you manage; follow API connection setup. The graphical Desktop installation keeps its internal credentials managed by its proxy—do not assume that it exposes a shell token.

From the example directory, with that daemon connection configured:

go run ../../tools/daemon-local -root ../.. -example scientific-workflows/montage-050 -wait=false

The command prints the submitted run ID and returns while execution continues. Connect Desktop to that same instance and open the run. Inspect its activity DAG, file handoffs, logs, and completion status. The daemon owns execution and transfers; the standalone runner's outputs/ directory belongs to the separate standalone path.

What the completed hybrid experiment observed​

The following results come from the preserved completion record for montage-docker-image-real-20261010-v2, dated by that run's identity. The real API-reported makespan was about 1.91× the planned estimate. That is an observation from this run, not a general slowdown factor. Close agreement between the plan and simulation did not establish that the real distributed execution would match either prediction.

The accompanying results record identifies whole-workspace traffic and different planned edge volumes as a comparability limit. Summed transfer or compute work can overlap across activities and is not the same as wall-clock makespan. Likewise, a zero reported interference value cannot establish that physical contention was absent.

The recorded cloud compute-and-boot-disk lifecycle estimate was USD 0.3532 at the experiment's list rates. It excludes network egress, public IPv4, reusable image storage, discounts, and tax, and assigns no calibrated monetary tariff to HPC. It is an estimate, not a provider invoice or a current price quote. Other cost fields in the JSON use different task/window scopes and should not be treated as equivalent bills.

What is—and is not—verified for the local bundle​

The checked-in local image contract was validated on 2026-10-20: twelve FITS inputs, 58 activities, and 138 named handoffs. That record explicitly states fullExecutionPerformed: false. Its separate daemon snapshot recorded a running workflow with zero completed activities at capture time. These are historical snapshots; neither establishes the current state of another instance.

The completed hybrid run supplies the mosaic and the results in this article. To claim a completed reproduction on your machine, retain your own successful validator output, activity records, and output manifest. The local showcase page links the checked-in contract and daemon evidence.
